object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account in the system, identified by a unique account number. The account is the primary entity to which subscriptions, products, and billing are attached.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.
Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: A unique six-digit identifier for an account, never reused even if an account closes and reopens.

source_references.excerpt: Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off... Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: An agreement that an account pays a specified amount on a billing cycle for a product. Each subscription is identified by a unique subscription ID and contains pricing, billing frequency, status, and date information.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID... Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a subscription, generated and prefixed with 'SUB'.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a subscription ID... Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product offering in the system, identified by a product code. Currently three products are available: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: A unique code identifying a product, one of: CORE, ANALYTICS, or CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: Priceplan
object_types.definition: A billing artifact that specifies the price a customer pays and the frequency of billing. Identified by a plan code (e.g., CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490). Each price plan entitles exactly one feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.
And I mean the billing artefact. The thing that generates the invoice line.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a price plan, specifying the product, billing period, and price in the code (e.g., CORE-MO-49).

source_references.excerpt: It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: A feature bundle representing a tier of service, identified by its name. Specifies what a customer gets: number of seats, API access, SSO, and other features. Examples: Starter, Professional, Enterprise.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO. It's the thing on the pricing page.
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me.

object_types.name: BundleName
object_types.definition: The name of a feature bundle, uniquely identifying it (e.g., Starter, Professional, Enterprise).

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, identified by a change ID. Captures the new price plan, effective date, and who requested the change. Enables historical tracking of what a customer was paying over time.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record... It's got a change ID... A plan change belongs to exactly one subscription? One change, one subscription. It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a plan change record.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID. It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription begins. Mandatory on every subscription.

source_references.excerpt: Start date... Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription ends. Optional; open-ended subscriptions have no end date and run until cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: End date, sometimes... An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The frequency at which a customer is billed for a subscription. Allowed values: Monthly or Annual. Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

source_references.excerpt: Billing period -- what are the values? Monthly or annual... Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The status of a subscription at a point in time. Allowed values: Trialing, Active, Past Due, Cancelled. Every subscription is in exactly one status.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled... Exactly one, yes.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect. May differ from the date the change was requested.

source_references.excerpt: when it takes effect, and those are different dates. Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month... the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: An identifier or name of the person or system that requested a plan change.

ambiguities.description: Plan terminology is overloaded: 'plan' refers to at least two distinct concepts in the model - (1) PriceplanArtifact (billing artifact, e.g., CORE-MO-49), and (2) FeatureBundle (feature tier, e.g., Professional). A third usage by the sales team (negotiated deal terms) is explicitly excluded from this model. The generic term 'plan' appears throughout the transcript and in business language but has been disambiguated in the model. Stakeholders acknowledge this terminological confusion will persist in casual conversation.

source_references.excerpt: Priya, what's a plan? [Priya explains pricing artifact] Tom: That's not what I mean by plan at all... When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise... [Sales team calls a third thing a plan]
Tom: Only that we still call three different things "plan" and this document won't fix that. Facilitator: It won't. But it'll at least name them separately, which is a start.

ambiguities.description: Paused status ambiguity: The transcript mentions a 'paused' flag that behaves like a subscription status but is stored and implemented as a separate boolean field, causing bugs. It is not included in the official four-status enumeration (Trialing, Active, Past Due, Cancelled) because Finance reports off those four. However, its interaction with the Active status is unclear: does a paused subscription still show as Active in reports, creating duplicate counting? This creates a potential data quality issue not modeled.

source_references.excerpt: Tom: There's also paused. Priya: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag... If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too... I'm not going to invent a fifth status you don't have. Priya: Please don't. Finance reports off those four.

ambiguities.description: Mid-term cancellation policy on annual subscriptions is unresolved: When a customer cancels an annual subscription mid-term after paying upfront, the system sets an end date to the paid-through date and access continues with no refund mechanism in the base system. However, four manual refunds were issued as 'goodwill' last quarter. Whether this represents an undocumented policy, a revenue recognition issue, or a business rule yet to be decided is not determined. The facilitator explicitly parked this as undecided and not to be modeled.

source_references.excerpt: Tom: Mid-term cancellation on annual plans... Priya: Nothing happens. They've paid for the year, they keep access until December, we don't refund... Tom: Four times in a quarter isn't goodwill, it's a policy nobody's written down... [Facilitator] What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: PlanChange requester identity and type: The 'requester' field on a plan change records 'who requested it' but the transcript does not clarify what type of identifier or identifier scheme is used (user ID, email, name, etc.). It is modeled as a text value type but its semantic meaning and format are not specified.

source_references.excerpt: we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates... It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

ambiguities.description: MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) derivation and reporting layer: MRR is stated to be derived from the price plan price and billing period (e.g., annual 490 becomes monthly 40.83). The facilitator explicitly decided not to model it as a stored attribute. However, it appears in Sam's reporting layer dashboards. The relationship between how it is computed, where it lives in the reporting layer, and whether it is cached or computed on-demand is not specified. This is noted as outside the scope of source system modeling.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR... It's on the subscription in the reporting layer... In the source system, is MRR a field somebody sets, or is it worked out? It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month... I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription, then, because it isn't a fact anybody asserts

ambiguities.description: Subscription current plan maintenance and consistency: Priya indicates the current_plan field on a subscription is 'denormalised' and 'maintained by the change process, nobody sets it by hand.' If current plan and plan change history ever disagree, change history wins and the current plan is the bug. The model captures both the current_plan fact and the PlanChange records, but does not formally express this consistency rule or the precedence relationship.

source_references.excerpt: it does have a current plan field... The changes are the history, but there's a denormalised current plan on the record. It's maintained by the change process, nobody sets it by hand... if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: Product offerings are fixed at three today but discovery phase has a fourth in progress: The ProductCode value constraint lists CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT as the current fixed set. However, Tom notes 'There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.' The model captures the current state; future product additions will require updating the value constraint. No time or versioning information is captured.

source_references.excerpt: We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT. Fixed at three? Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: FeatureBundle identification by name: Bundles are identified by a name (Starter, Professional, Enterprise) which 'annoys' Tom because there is no machine-readable code. The natural language name is treated as the reference_mode, which is unusual but matches the stakeholder statement. If bundles are later given codes, or if naming conventions change, identification must be revisited.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me... Is the name unique? Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

ambiguities.description: Legacy plan retirement: Priya mentions 'sometimes a legacy one we haven't retired' price plan, suggesting plans can become obsolete or inactive. The model does not capture plan lifecycle state (active, retired, etc.) or temporal constraints on which plans new subscriptions can use.

source_references.excerpt: There's a monthly and an annual for each bundle, and sometimes a legacy one we haven't retired.

ambiguities.description: Enterprise bespoke pricing: Priya states 'there are price plans that exist only for one customer. Bespoke enterprise pricing.' The model does not capture whether a price plan is bespoke to a single customer or shared, which could be important for pricing audits and customer-specific reporting.

source_references.excerpt: And there are price plans that exist only for one customer. Bespoke enterprise pricing. Those still point at a bundle.

ambiguities.description: Account reopening and historical continuity: When an account closes and the same company later reopens, Priya stated 'they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting.' From a product perspective, Tom notes 'it's the same company and we lose the history.' The model does not capture a relationship between the old and new accounts, nor a way to group closed and reopened accounts for analysis. This is a deliberate business choice (for revenue recognition) but may cause data continuity questions.

source_references.excerpt: Six digits, sequential, never reused. If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting... From a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.
